title: Paginate with stable ordering (PostgreSQL)
description: Compare offset pages with a composite cursor, handle tied timestamps, and fetch one extra row.

steps.label: Numbered pages
steps.title: Give each row a stable position
steps.body:
This guide uses PostgreSQL and Drizzle ORM **1.0.0-rc.5**. Six posts include several tied timestamps. Sort by both `createdAt` and the unique `id`, then use `limit` and `offset`. Page numbers start at one, so the offset is `(page - 1) * pageSize`.

Press **Run**. Pages contain IDs 1–2, 3–4 and 5–6. Ordering only by the timestamp would leave tied rows without a defined relative order. The schema includes a matching composite index.

PostgreSQL stores `createdAt` as `timestamptz`; string mode keeps the database timestamp available for the cursor.

meta.summary: Use a unique tie-breaker before dividing rows into numbered pages.
meta.changed: Three pages return every seeded post once, in timestamp and ID order.

steps.label: Rows can shift
steps.title: Insert before the next offset page
steps.body:
The first request reads IDs 1 and 2. Before the second request, an insert adds a post ahead of them in the sort order.

Press **Run**. Offset 2 now returns IDs 2 and 3: ID 2 appears again because row positions moved. A unique order makes each query deterministic; it does not freeze the dataset between requests.

Each Run starts from the seed again. This step simulates two requests and one intervening write within a single execution.

meta.summary: See an offset page repeat a row after an earlier insert.
meta.changed: The second request repeats ID 2 after the insert shifts row positions.

steps.label: Cursor ties
steps.title: A timestamp alone skips tied rows
steps.body:
A cursor describes where the previous page ended. The tempting filter is `createdAt > last.createdAt`.

Press **Run**. The first page contains IDs 1 and 2, but ID 3 shares their timestamp. The timestamp-only filter jumps to IDs 4 and 5, skipping ID 3.

The cursor must describe the same complete ordering as the query. Here that means both the timestamp and the ID.

meta.summary: Demonstrate why a cursor must include the unique tie-breaker.
meta.changed: ID 3 is skipped because its timestamp equals the last row of page one.

steps.label: Composite cursor
steps.title: Continue after the complete sort key
steps.body:
Open `pagination.ts`. The filter keeps rows with a later timestamp, or the same timestamp and a larger ID. `Cursor` derives both field types from the table. The comparisons match the ascending order.

The helper fetches `pageSize + 1` rows. The extra row determines `hasNextPage`, but is not returned. The next cursor comes from the last **returned** row, so the extra row appears on the following page.

Press **Run**. All six posts appear once, including the ties. The final page has `hasNextPage: false` and `nextCursor: null`. Validate positive page sizes and cursor values at your application's input boundary before calling a helper like this.

meta.summary: Keep tied timestamps and compute hasNextPage from one extra row.
meta.changed: Pages return IDs 1–2, 3–4 and 5–6; the last page has no next cursor.

steps.label: Use the starters
steps.title: Choose numbered pages or sequential navigation
steps.body:
Offset pagination lets you jump to a page number. Cursor pagination continues from a known sort key and can avoid scanning a growing offset when a suitable index is used. This small dataset demonstrates correctness, not a performance benchmark.

A cursor is not a snapshot: deleting rows, changing sort keys or changing filters between requests still changes what you see. Reuse the same filters and ordering with a cursor. Descending order also needs the matching reversed comparisons.

Open either complete starter below to edit it without the deliberate mistakes from the guide.

meta.summary: Use the direct examples and keep cursor stability separate from snapshot guarantees.
